course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

topic.title: The Development of an American Culture
topic.summary: How a national culture emerged between 1800 and 1848 from American subjects, European influences, and regional traditions, and how Romantic ideas shaped literature, art, philosophy, and architecture.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes the new national culture that emerged in the United States in the early 1800s?
choices: It rejected every European style and idea and relied only on Native American traditions
It combined American elements, European influences, and regional traditions
It was created almost entirely by a federal arts program that Congress had established
It replaced all regional differences with a single uniform culture in every part of the country
questions.explanation: Americans drew on their own experience and landscape, borrowed from Europe, and kept regional sensibilities.
choiceExplanations: American artists and writers still borrowed European styles.
Americans drew on their own experience and landscape, borrowed from Europe, and kept regional sensibilities.
No federal arts program of this kind existed.
Regional cultures remained distinct.
questions.distinguisher: The Native American traditions choice is close because American subjects mattered, but artists continued to rely on European forms.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: The painters of the Hudson River School, such as Thomas Cole, are known for
choices: portraits of the founders of the nation painted in the style of ancient Rome
scenes of crowded factories and the working conditions of the new mill towns
battle scenes from the War of 1812 that praised the nation's military leaders
landscapes that celebrated the grandeur of the American wilderness
questions.explanation: Hudson River School artists expressed the Romantic view that nature was a source of beauty and national pride.
choiceExplanations: The Hudson River School painted landscapes.
These painters celebrated nature and did not stress industry.
Their subject was nature and not battles.
Hudson River School artists expressed the Romantic view that nature was a source of beauty and national pride.
questions.distinguisher: The founders choice is close because American artists did paint portraits, but the Hudson River School focused on landscape.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Romanticism, which influenced American writers and artists, emphasized
choices: emotion, imagination, individualism, and a reverence for nature
reason, order, and the rules of classical models for art and literature
obedience to tradition and to the authority of established churches and rulers
scientific measurement of social problems and the use of statistics in public policy
questions.explanation: Romantic writers and artists valued feeling, imagination, and the individual over strict rules and rationalism.
choiceExplanations: Romantic writers and artists valued feeling, imagination, and the individual over strict rules and rationalism.
That describes the Enlightenment and its classical ideals.
Romanticism stressed individualism.
Romanticism stressed feeling more than measurement.
questions.distinguisher: The reason and order choice is close because the Enlightenment shaped the founding era, but Romanticism reacted against it.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Transcendentalists such as Emerson and Thoreau argued that
choices: truth could be found only through scientific reasoning and the study of social institutions
religious authorities should guide all moral decisions in public and private life
individuals could find truth through intuition and nature and should not simply conform
the government should direct the arts and require schools to teach a national literature
questions.explanation: Emerson's “Self-Reliance” urged people to trust themselves, and Thoreau also valued nature and independence from society's demands.
choiceExplanations: Transcendentalists trusted intuition more than institutions.
They stressed the judgment of the individual.
Emerson's “Self-Reliance” urged people to trust themselves, and Thoreau also valued nature and independence from society's demands.
They distrusted conformity and government direction.
questions.distinguisher: The scientific reasoning choice is close because the age valued science, but Transcendentalists emphasized intuition.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why many American writers and artists chose American landscapes and history as subjects after 1815?
choices: A federal law that required artists to portray American subjects in all public works
A growing desire to define a national identity distinct from Europe
A refusal by European governments to allow their art to enter the United States
A decline in interest in nature as the growth of cities drew attention to factories
questions.explanation: After the War of 1812, national pride encouraged artists to look for American themes.
choiceExplanations: No such law existed.
After the War of 1812, national pride encouraged artists to look for American themes.
European art and ideas continued to circulate.
Interest in nature grew in these decades.
questions.distinguisher: The federal law choice is close because government sometimes commissioned art, but the shift came from national feeling.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: The popularity of Greek Revival architecture for public buildings is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A rule that required every state capitol to copy the design of the national Capitol
A rejection of European styles in favor of buildings modeled on Native American designs
The need for fireproof buildings after the burning of Washington in the War of 1812
Americans' view of ancient Greece and Rome as models of democracy and republican virtue for the new nation
questions.explanation: Columns and pediments linked the young republic to classical models that Americans admired.
choiceExplanations: No such rule existed.
Greek Revival drew on classical Europe.
The style reflected ideals and not fire safety.
Columns and pediments linked the young republic to classical models that Americans admired.
questions.distinguisher: The Capitol rule choice is close because federal buildings influenced style, but no rule required copying.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a similarity between Romanticism and Transcendentalism?
choices: Both valued the individual, intuition or emotion, and the natural world
Both relied mainly on reason and the rules of classical models in art and thought
Both accepted the authority of established churches and inherited traditions
Both were created in the United States by writers who had no contact with Europe
questions.explanation: Transcendentalism grew out of Romanticism and shared its stress on individualism and nature.
choiceExplanations: Transcendentalism grew out of Romanticism and shared its stress on individualism and nature.
Both reacted against strict rationalism.
Both stressed individual judgment.
Romanticism came from Europe.
questions.distinguisher: The reason and classical rules choice is close because the Enlightenment came before both, but both rejected its strictness.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The Romantic belief in human perfectibility is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: A belief that human nature was fixed at birth and could not be changed by education
A claim that science had already explained all human behavior and had solved social problems
A belief that individuals and society could be improved, which encouraged many reform movements of the era
A government plan to improve public schools through a national system of examinations
questions.explanation: Many Americans believed that people and institutions could be improved, which inspired reformers.
choiceExplanations: Perfectibility meant that people could improve.
Romantic thought did not rest on that claim.
Many Americans believed that people and institutions could be improved, which inspired reformers.
No national plan of this kind existed.
questions.distinguisher: The fixed human nature choice is close because it reflects the older Calvinist view, but Romantics believed in improvement.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a specific historical development or process is situated within a broader historical context.

questions.prompt: Noah Webster's dictionary (1828) reflected a desire to
choices: replace English with a new national language that all citizens would be taught
establish a distinctly American form of the English language
adopt British spelling and usage in all textbooks used in American schools
teach American children to read ancient Greek and Latin in the early grades
questions.explanation: Webster's spelling books and dictionary supported a sense of American cultural independence.
choiceExplanations: Webster promoted American English, not a new language.
Webster's spelling books and dictionary supported a sense of American cultural independence.
Webster promoted American spellings and usage.
His work concerned American English.
questions.distinguisher: The new language choice is close because Webster wanted a national tongue, but it was a form of English.
